title: Numbers, progressions and transposing
summary: Use the number system to play any progression in any key, transpose for a singer or choir, and learn the gospel moves built on 2-5-1. Project: one song in three keys.

videos.title: Learn music theory in half an hour (Andrew Huang)
Music theory for dum-dums, full beginner course (Piano With Corey)

practice.question: The worship leader says "1-5-6-4 in G". Which chords do you play?
practice.explanation: G major is G A B C D E F#. 1 = G, 5 = D, 6 = E, 4 = C. The 6 chord is minor in a major key, so it is Em: G D Em C.

practice.question: Why can so many hymns and simple songs be played with only the 1, 4 and 5 chords?
options: They are the only major chords that sound good
The melody always uses only three notes
They are the only chords with no black keys
Together they contain every note of the major scale
practice.explanation: In C: C E G + F A C + G B D = C D E F G A B, the whole scale. So one of the three fits under almost any melody note.

practice.question: In any major key, which numbers give minor chords?
practice.explanation: The pattern is 1 major, 2 minor, 3 minor, 4 major, 5 major, 6 minor, 7 diminished. In C: Dm, Em and Am are the minor ones.

practice.question: A YouTube teacher writes I-V-vi-IV. What is that in the number system?
practice.explanation: I = 1, V = 5, vi = 6, IV = 4. The small letters (vi) show the chord is minor; the numbers are the same idea.

practice.title: Move a progression to a new key

practice.question: You're working out a song. It keeps resting on a D chord, ends on D, and you also hear G, A and Em. What key is it most likely in?
practice.explanation: Home is where the song rests and ends: D. D major has D, Em, F#m, G, A, Bm, so D (1), G (4), A (5) and Em (2) all fit.

practice.question: The song is in E (E B C#m A) and the soloist asks for it a whole step lower. What do you play?
practice.explanation: Down a whole step is down 2 half steps: E->D, B->A, C#->B, A->G. The minor chord stays minor, so C#m becomes Bm: D A Bm G.

practice.question: The choir sings in Ab and the director wants the last chorus up a half step. What is the new key, and what happens to the numbers?
options: A, and every minor chord becomes major
Bb, and the numbers stay the same
A, and the numbers stay the same
practice.explanation: Ab up one half step is A. Transposing never changes the numbers or qualities, only the starting point.

The most popular chord progression ever: 2-5-1 (YousicPlay)

practice.question: In C, the chain Em-Am-Dm-G-C sounds like it keeps pulling forward. Why?
options: Each root moves up a half step
Each root falls a fifth (up a fourth) to the next
The chords are all in root position
practice.explanation: E->A, A->D, D->G, G->C: each move is down a fifth, the strongest root movement. That is the 3-6-2-5-1 chain.

practice.question: What is the difference between G7 and Gmaj7?
options: G7 has F, Gmaj7 has F#
G7 is minor, Gmaj7 is major
G7 has four notes, Gmaj7 has three
practice.explanation: Both are G B D plus a seventh. G7 adds F (10 half steps up), the dominant 7 used on the 5 chord. Gmaj7 adds F# (11 half steps up).

practice.question: The song is in Eb. Which is the 2-5-1 with sevenths?
practice.explanation: Eb major is Eb F G Ab Bb C D. 2 = F, 5 = Bb, 1 = Eb, with the pattern m7, 7, maj7: Fm7 Bb7 Ebmaj7.

project.title: One song in three keys
checklist: Chose a song and found its key note by ear
Wrote every section of the song as numbers, with the section order
Wrote the chord names in the original key
Wrote the chord names in a higher key and a lower key
Played one section with sevenths (maj7, m7, 7)
Played a 2-5-1 leading into a section
Played the song at full tempo in all three keys
Recorded all three versions back to back
